an0073.user: No-code SaaS, acquiring via WhatsApp broadcasts. I want the non-obvious read. Over 8 weeks I scaled spend from ₹6L to ₹13.7L. CAC went ₹453 to ₹776, ROAS dropped 2.4 to 1.4. AOV ₹1,100, margin 59%. On paper I scaled and it feels like it backfired — what am I not seeing?
an0073.assistant:
What you're not seeing is that you've crossed from profit into loss, and the scaling itself is the cause.

Contribution per order: at the start, ₹1,100 × 59% − ₹453 = ₹649 − ₹453 = +₹196. Today, ₹649 − ₹776 = −₹127. You went from making ₹196 a customer to losing ₹127 on each — and the only lever you pulled was more than doubling spend. It didn't backfire randomly; it backfired mechanically.

The non-obvious bit is why more money made things worse. Your cheapest customers are the warm ones — people already engaged with your WhatsApp list, close to converting. That's a finite pool. The first ₹6L harvested them at ₹453. To deploy ₹13.7L you had to push into colder audiences who need far more convincing, and cold reach always costs more — hence CAC climbing to ₹776 and ROAS sliding to 1.4. The channel has an efficient ceiling, and you drove ₹7.7L straight past it into negative territory.

The fix is not 'optimise the ads.' Pull spend back to where CAC sat under your ₹649 breakeven — roughly the old ₹6L zone where you made ₹196. Then earn the right to scale again by manufacturing new cheap demand: new audience sources, fresh creative angles, a second acquisition channel to refill the warm pool. More budget into a saturated channel doesn't buy growth — it buys losses. Raise the ceiling before you spend toward it again.

an0074.user: Jewellery brand, Google Search. I want a sharp answer, not the obvious one: why is my CTR low? Last 30 days — 970K impressions, 11,656 clicks so CTR ~1.2%, but only 84 orders, which is a 0.72% conversion rate. AOV ₹1,500, on broad-match keywords.
an0074.assistant:
The sharp answer is that CTR is the wrong number to be asking about, and chasing it would deepen the actual problem.

Look at the real wound: 11,656 clicks, 84 orders, 0.72% conversion. Nearly twelve thousand people clicked and almost none bought. That's not an ad-interest failure — your 1.2% CTR is fine — it's an intent failure. Broad-match is casting your jewellery ad across loosely related searches: 'gold rate today', 'jewellery designs', 'how to clean silver'. Those people click out of curiosity and leave, because they were never shopping to buy.

So if you 'fixed' CTR, you'd just buy more of the wrong clicks faster. The lever runs the opposite way. Kill broad-match; move to phrase and exact match on genuine purchase intent — '[your style] necklace buy online', 'gold earrings under ₹X', your branded terms. Build a hard negative-keyword list to block the window-shopping queries draining ₹ on every click. Expect your click volume to fall and your conversion rate to climb — that's the trade you want.

Stop optimising for clicks. At ₹1,500 AOV you can't afford 12,000 browsers; you need 2,000 buyers. Chase intent, and the 0.72% takes care of itself.

an0076.user: Amazon marketplace seller, also running a Meta + Google mix. Here's the dump, what's wrong: AOV ₹800, gross margin 26%, CAC ₹429, ROAS 1.9, CTR 2.4%. My real question — how do I lower my CAC? That feels like the thing to fix.
an0076.assistant:
CAC isn't your problem, and lowering it won't save you — your margin is the problem, and it's bleeding you on every order regardless of the ads.

Do the contribution math: ₹800 × 26% − ₹429 = ₹208 − ₹429 = −₹221. You lose ₹221 on every single sale. Sit with that, because it changes everything: even if you were brilliant and cut CAC by ₹100, you'd still lose ₹121 an order. There is no CAC low enough to rescue a 26% gross margin at an ₹800 AOV — the gross profit per order (₹208) doesn't even cover the cost of acquiring the customer. The ads aren't broken; the unit economics are.

This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume, and it's the most common way founders misdiagnose a struggling store. You're asking 'how do I lower CAC' because that's the knob ads dashboards show you, while the real leak is upstream of the ad entirely.

Three levers, and none of them are 'the ads':
- Margin: renegotiate COGS, cut packaging/shipping waste, or drop the worst-margin SKUs. Getting 26% to 40% turns that ₹208 into ₹320 and you're suddenly breakeven-plus.
- AOV: bundles, a higher-priced hero product, a minimum-cart nudge. ₹800 → ₹1,200 at even 30% margin is ₹360 gross, covering the ₹429... almost — which tells you both levers need to move.
- Pricing: if the market allows ₹950 instead of ₹800, that's pure margin.

Fix the economics first. A profitable product with mediocre ads beats a loss-making product with perfect ones every time. The ad account is the last thing to touch here.

That last part is the whole diagnosis. Frequency 3.4 with a sliding CTR, against unchanged creative and audience, is textbook creative fatigue. Above ~2.5, frequency means the same people keep seeing the same ad; at 3.4 they've seen it enough to stop noticing, so clicks fall and you pay more to keep serving an ad people now scroll past. It isn't the algorithm and it isn't your targeting — both are constant, which is exactly why neither can be the cause. an0079.user: Pet-care brand, running YouTube. I'd like the considered read on an attribution puzzle. Post-iOS, the platform reports 4.5 ROAS while Shopify last-click shows 1.8. ₹8.5L spent last month. I know they measure differently, but practically — how do I actually run my budget when the two numbers are this far apart?
an0079.assistant:
You run it off a third number that neither dashboard can spin — because trying to budget off either 4.5 or 1.8 is what's got you stuck.

Quick why, since you already know the gist: the platform's 4.5 over-credits (post-iOS modelling plus a 7-day-click window means it claims sales it only influenced), and last-click's 1.8 under-credits (it hands the whole sale to the final touch — usually a brand search or direct visit — and gives your YouTube ad nothing for creating the demand). YouTube especially gets robbed by last-click, because it's an upper-funnel, demand-generating channel; people rarely buy straight off a video, they buy days later through another door. So your truth almost certainly sits closer to the middle-to-high end, but you can't prove exactly where, and you don't need to.

Here's how you actually budget: anchor on blended CAC. Total spend — ₹8.5L — divided by your real new-customer count from Shopify for the month. That's the honest, all-in cost to buy a customer. Set a target blended CAC based on what a pet-care customer is worth (first order plus their reorder value), and manage spend up or down to hold that target. The two ROAS figures become diagnostic colour, not the steering wheel.

If you later need to know how much YouTube specifically deserves, run a geo holdout — turn it off in a few regions for a few weeks and watch blended sales. That's the only clean read on incrementality. Until then: blended CAC is your budget metric. Manage to it weekly.

an0084.user: Home-care brand, Meta ads. My conversion rate looks low so I'm sure my ad creative is the problem — I need better ads, right? That's where I'd put my effort.
an0084.assistant:
Maybe — but a 'low conversion rate' can break at three completely different points, and only one of them is the creative. Jumping to 'better ads' without locating the actual drop is how founders pour effort into the wrong stage. Pull your last 30 days as four numbers first:

- Visits → add-to-cart. If this is weak, then yes, the issue is upstream — the ad or the product page isn't selling, and your creative instinct is right.
- Add-to-cart → reached checkout. A drop here is a price or shipping shock, not an ad problem — better creative won't touch it.
- Reached checkout → purchase. A drop here is checkout friction — forced login, no UPI, no COD — and no amount of new creative fixes a broken payment step.

The stage with the steepest fall is where your effort belongs. If the leak is at add-to-cart, rebuild the creative. If it's at checkout, leave the ads alone and fix the store.
